Studying the reproductive physiology of Longhead flathead (Leviprora inops) under controlled conditions has yielded important baseline data. At a stable water temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was measured at 5% [GSI = 5%]. This value suggests that reproductive investment may be finely tuned to local environmental conditions, with the species potentially adopting a conservative energetic strategy. The thermal regime at which these observations were made is typical of the deeper coastal waters the species inhabits, and it likely influences the timing of gametogenesis. Such measurements are crucial for understanding the interplay between temperature and reproductive output in this benthic predator.

In the early stages of development, the age at birth for Leviprora inops has been documented as 10 days [ab = 10 days] when eggs are incubated at 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C]. The newly emerged prolarvae are initially lecithotrophic and possess a modest wet weight at birth of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a value derived from the estimated egg dimensions. This minimal initial mass reflects the small yolk reserves available to the developing embryo, which must rapidly transition to exogenous feeding. The precise timing of eclosion and the size of the yolk-sac larva are critical determinants of early survival, dictating the window during which the larva must successfully capture its first prey.

As individuals progress through the pelagic larval phase and undergo larval metamorphosis, they eventually settle to a demersal lifestyle. Upon reaching sexual maturation, the total length at puberty has been recorded at 27 cm [Lp = 27 cm], marking the point at which individuals are capable of reproductive activity. This size threshold is notably lower than the species' ultimate total length, which has been determined to be 52.1 cm [Li = 52.1 cm], indicating a prolonged period of post-pubertal somatic growth. Achieving this ultimate length likely requires several years of successful foraging, and the considerable gap between the length at puberty and the maximum length suggests that older, larger individuals contribute disproportionately to the spawning stock.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown Longhead flathead has been estimated at 767 grams [Wwi = 767 grams], a value consistent with the length-weight relationship established for this species. This maximum recorded adult mass represents the end point of a growth trajectory that is strongly influenced by food availability and thermal conditions. In comparison, the length at puberty of 27 cm corresponds to a considerably lower body mass, emphasizing the substantial energetic investment required to progress from the onset of maturity to the achievement of asymptotic size. The species' relatively large ultimate size likely confers advantages in terms of fecundity and competitive dominance on the fishing grounds.

Regarding the species' maximum longevity, field records indicate a life span of 7,665 days [am = 7,665 days] for individuals maintained at a temperature of 17.7 °C [T = 17.7 °C], which is equivalent to approximately 21 years. This extended lifespan is characteristic of a slow life-history pace, with individuals investing in somatic maintenance over many years. Such a long reproductive window allows for multiple spawning events across a lifetime, which buffers the population against years of poor recruitment.
